title: Valium and Alcohol: Why Diazepam Makes Drinking Riskier
excerpt: Why Valium (diazepam) and alcohol are a dangerous mix, why diazepam stays in your system for days, what to do about flying, and the warning signs that need 911.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Valium (diazepam)? How the two interact, why diazepam lingers for days, how long to wait, flying advice, and overdose warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking Valium (diazepam). Valium and alcohol both slow the brain down through the same calming system, and together they can cause heavy sedation, blackouts, falls, dangerously slow breathing, and in the worst cases coma or death. What makes Valium different from many other anxiety medicines is how long it lasts. Diazepam and the active substance your body turns it into can stay in your system for days, so "I took it yesterday" doesn't mean it's gone. Most people who mix the two once won't end up in the hospital, but there is no amount known to be safe, and the risk is hard to predict in advance.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on a day you take Valium, and be cautious about drinking for at least a day or two after your last dose, longer if you take it regularly or you're older. Never take Valium after you've been drinking, including to calm hangover anxiety. If you've been given Valium for a flight, skip the airplane drinks. Never take a "Valium" pill that didn't come from a pharmacy, because counterfeit pills can contain other drugs, including fentanyl. If someone has combined the two and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or has blue or gray lips, **call 911 right away.**

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how Valium and alcohol interact and what the official labeling says. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and it does not give dosing advice. **Talk to your prescriber** about alcohol before you start Valium, if you've already been drinking while taking it, or if you want to stop either one. **Call 911 immediately if** someone who has mixed Valium and alcohol can't be woken, is breathing slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. In the US, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222** for non-emergency questions.

## How Valium and Alcohol Interact: The Brain Chemistry in Plain Words

Valium is the best-known brand name for **diazepam**, a medicine in the **benzodiazepine** family. It has been around since the 1960s and is prescribed for several different reasons: anxiety, muscle spasms, certain seizure problems, and, under close medical supervision, managing alcohol withdrawal. Doctors also sometimes prescribe a small supply for one-off situations like a fear of flying or a medical procedure. Other members of the same family include Xanax (alprazolam), Ativan (lorazepam), and Klonopin (clonazepam).

To understand why Valium and alcohol are a risky pair, you need one piece of brain chemistry.

Your brain has a built-in brake pedal called **GABA**. It's a chemical messenger that calms nerve cells down. When GABA attaches to its main receptor, called the **GABA-A receptor**, it makes the nerve cell less likely to fire. That's what produces feelings of calm, relaxation, and, in larger amounts, sleepiness.

**Valium presses harder on that brake.** Benzodiazepines attach to the GABA-A receptor and make it respond more strongly to the GABA that's already there. That's how they ease anxiety and relax muscles.

**Alcohol presses the same brake, in a different way.** Alcohol also boosts GABA-A activity, and at the same time it dampens **glutamate**, the brain's main "go" signal. Less "go" and more "stop" is why drinking makes you relaxed, then clumsy, then sleepy.

When you combine the two, they don't simply take turns. They both push on the same receptor from different angles, and the result can be **stronger than either one alone would suggest.** Doctors describe this as additive or synergistic central nervous system depression. In everyday terms, a dose of Valium you tolerate well and a few drinks you'd normally handle can together make you far more sedated, confused, and uncoordinated than you expect.

The part of the brain that worries doctors most is the **brainstem**, which runs automatic functions like breathing. In high enough combined amounts, the brakes get applied there too, and breathing can become slow and shallow. That's the mechanism behind most deaths involving sedatives and alcohol.

## Why Valium Is Different: It Lasts a Very Long Time

If you read our guides on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) or [Ativan and alcohol](/never-hungover/ativan-and-alcohol), the brain chemistry above will sound familiar. What sets Valium apart is its timeline.

Diazepam is one of the **longest-acting** benzodiazepines in common use. Two things drive that:

1. **Diazepam itself has a long half-life.** The half-life is how long it takes your body to clear half of a dose. The prescribing information for diazepam describes a half-life of up to about two days in healthy adults, and it can be longer in some people.
2. **Your liver turns it into another active drug.** As your liver breaks diazepam down, it produces **desmethyldiazepam** (also called nordiazepam), which also calms the brain and lasts even longer, with a half-life the label describes as up to about 100 hours. Diazepam is processed mainly by the liver enzymes known as CYP3A4 and CYP2C19.

In plain words: a single Valium tablet doesn't vanish overnight. Some of it, and some of its active by-product, is still on board the next day and often the day after. And if you take Valium regularly, the drug **builds up** over the first week or two until it reaches a steady level in your blood.

This matters for drinking in three ways:

- **"Wait until tomorrow" isn't a reliable plan.** With a short-acting drug, waiting overnight clears much of it. With Valium, you may still have meaningful amounts in your system the next evening.
- **Older adults clear it even more slowly.** The diazepam label notes that its half-life gets longer with age, and older people are also more prone to falls and confusion. A drink that would be harmless on its own can tip an older person on Valium into a fall.
- **Liver problems slow it down further.** Because the liver does the work, anyone with liver disease, including liver damage from heavy drinking, may hold onto diazepam much longer.

Klonopin is the other long-lasting member of the family people often ask about. Our article on [Klonopin and alcohol](/never-hungover/klonopin-and-alcohol) covers a similar next-day problem.

## Diazepam and Alcohol: Same Drug, Same Risk

People search for "diazepam and alcohol" and "Valium and alcohol" as if they might be different questions. They aren't. Diazepam is the medicine; Valium is one brand name for it. Generic diazepam tablets, liquids, rectal gels used for seizures (such as Diastat), and nasal sprays (such as Valtoco) all contain the same drug and carry the same warnings about alcohol.

A few practical notes about the different forms:

- **Generic diazepam tablets** come in different strengths, and a pharmacy may switch manufacturers between refills. The tablet may look different, but the drug and the alcohol warning are the same.
- **Rescue forms for seizures** (rectal gel and nasal spray) are given during an emergency, often by a family member. If someone who received one has also been drinking, they need close watching and possibly emergency care.
- **Diazepam prescribed for muscle spasms** is still a benzodiazepine. People sometimes think of it as "just a muscle relaxer," but it acts on the brain exactly as it does when prescribed for anxiety. Our guide to [muscle relaxers and alcohol](/never-hungover/muscle-relaxers-and-alcohol) covers the other drugs in that category.

## What the Official Labeling Says

The US prescribing information for diazepam carries an **FDA boxed warning**, the agency's strongest kind. It warns that combining benzodiazepines with opioids can cause profound sedation, slowed breathing, coma, and death, and it also warns about abuse, misuse, addiction, physical dependence, and withdrawal reactions.

Alcohol is addressed in the label's warnings about other **central nervous system depressants**. The label tells patients to avoid alcohol while taking diazepam, because combining them increases sedation and the risk of slowed breathing. The patient Medication Guide says the same in plainer words: don't drink alcohol, and don't drive or operate machinery until you know how diazepam affects you.

The logic behind the opioid warning applies directly to alcohol. Two substances that slow breathing are more dangerous together than either one alone. Alcohol just isn't a prescription, so it's handled in the warnings rather than the box.

## Does Alcohol Change How Much Valium Is in Your Blood?

Besides the shared brain effect, there's some evidence of a second kind of interaction. Older research has suggested that drinking alcohol at the same time as taking diazepam can raise the amount of diazepam that reaches the blood, possibly by speeding absorption from the gut or by competing for the liver's attention. Findings have varied between studies, and this effect is probably smaller than the direct "two brakes" problem.

The practical takeaway doesn't change. You can't reliably predict how strongly the combination will hit you on a given night, because so many things shift it: your dose, how long you've been taking Valium, how much and how fast you drink, whether you've eaten, your body size, your age, and any other medicines you take.

## How Long After Taking Valium Can You Drink?

This is the most common question, and it doesn't have a single safe number. Because of the long half-life described above, the honest answer is **longer than you'd think, and longer than for most other anxiety pills.**

Here's how to think about it:

- **If you take Valium every day,** there's no window in the day when it's out of your system. Drinking means drinking on Valium. Talk to your prescriber about whether any alcohol is acceptable for you; for many people the answer will be no.
- **If you took a single dose, for example for a flight or a procedure,** the strongest effects fade within hours, but the drug and its active by-product linger for days. Many clinicians would advise avoiding alcohol for at least 24 to 48 hours after a single dose, and longer if you're older, have liver problems, or took a larger dose. Ask the person who prescribed it for advice that fits you.
- **If you take it "as needed" a few times a week,** the doses can overlap and build up. Treat yourself as being on it continuously.

And the reverse matters too. **Don't take Valium after you've been drinking.** Alcohol leaves the body at roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies a lot from person to person. Our guide on [how long alcohol stays in your system](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-in-your-system) explains the timeline. If you still feel drunk or tipsy, alcohol is still in your blood.

## Valium for Fear of Flying: Skip the Airplane Drinks

A common reason people end up asking about Valium and alcohol is a flight. Someone gets a few diazepam tablets from their doctor to take the edge off a fear of flying, then wonders whether a glass of wine on the plane is okay.

It isn't a good idea, for several reasons:

- **The combination is more sedating than either alone,** and you may not realize how impaired you are until you stand up, try to find your connecting gate, or need to follow crew instructions in an emergency.
- **Altitude and cabin conditions can make alcohol feel stronger** for some people, and a long flight often means drinking on an empty stomach and with little water.
- **You'll still have Valium on board when you land.** If you're driving from the airport, picking up a rental car, or drinking at your destination that evening, the diazepam from your morning dose is still working.
- **Deep sedation on a long flight** means sitting still for hours. Doctors generally advise people on long flights to move around and stay hydrated, which is harder to do when heavily sedated.

If flying is a real struggle, it's worth telling your prescriber how you plan to travel, including connections and what you'll do on arrival, so they can advise on timing. Some people find that a fear-of-flying course or talking therapy helps more over the long run than a pill. And on the travel day itself, water, food, and no alcohol make a sedative safer.

## Using Valium for Hangover Anxiety: Why It's a Bad Idea

Some people have a leftover Valium tablet and think about taking it the morning after heavy drinking to calm the jittery, anxious feeling people call "hangxiety." Please don't. There are three problems:

1. **Alcohol may still be in your blood.** After a long night, you can still have alcohol in your system the next morning, so you'd be combining the two after all.
2. **Hangover anxiety is partly a rebound from alcohol itself.** While you drink, alcohol boosts GABA and dampens glutamate. As it wears off, the brain swings the other way, which can leave you jittery, anxious, and sleeping poorly. Our guide to [hangxiety and what's behind it](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains this in detail. Covering that rebound with a long-acting sedative builds a pattern where you rely on one depressant to handle the after-effects of another.
3. **It can hide something you need to notice.** Shakiness, sweating, and a pounding heart after drinking are usually ordinary hangover symptoms (see our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes)). But in someone who drinks heavily every day, the same signs can be early **alcohol withdrawal**, which can become medically serious. Diazepam is in fact one of the drugs hospitals use to treat alcohol withdrawal, but that's done with monitoring and planned doses, not with a leftover tablet at home. If you think you might be in withdrawal, see a doctor or go to urgent care.

If hangover anxiety is a regular thing for you, the fixes that actually help are the plain ones: fewer drinks, drinking more slowly, eating, water, and sleep. Our article on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) covers how the two feed each other.

## Blackouts, Falls, and Risky Behavior

Benzodiazepines can cause **anterograde amnesia**, which means trouble forming new memories while the drug is active. Alcohol does the same thing, and blackouts happen when blood alcohol rises quickly. Together, they make memory gaps far more likely, even at amounts that wouldn't cause a blackout on their own. Our guide to [blackouts from drinking](/never-hungover/blackout-drunk) explains what's happening in the brain.

A blackout isn't just embarrassing. During one, people still walk, talk, drive, and make decisions, but with poor judgment and no record of what happened. Combined with the loss of coordination both substances cause, that's how injuries happen:

- **Falls and head injuries**, especially in older adults or anyone on a higher dose
- **Driving while impaired.** Both alcohol and diazepam impair driving, and the combination is worse. Because Valium lasts so long, you can be impaired the next morning without feeling it.
- **Choking on vomit** while deeply sedated
- **Being unable to protect yourself** in an unsafe situation

## Signs of a Dangerous Reaction (Call 911)

Most people who mix Valium and a small amount of alcohol will feel very drowsy and unsteady and then sleep it off. But some won't, and it's hard to tell in advance which group someone is in. Call 911 if someone who has combined them:

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses
- Is making gurgling or snoring sounds and can't be roused
- Has blue or gray lips or fingertips, or cold, clammy skin
- Has a very slow pulse
- Is having a seizure
- Is vomiting while drowsy or confused

**While you wait for help:** stay with them. If they're breathing but not responding, roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower, which doesn't reverse sedation. If there's any chance opioids or a non-pharmacy pill are involved, give **naloxone** (Narcan) if you have it. Naloxone doesn't reverse benzodiazepines or alcohol, but it can reverse an opioid that may be hidden in a counterfeit pill, and it's safe to give.

## Counterfeit Pills: A Real and Growing Risk

Pills sold outside pharmacies as "Valium," "diazepam," or "Xanax" are a serious danger. Public health agencies, including the US Drug Enforcement Administration, have repeatedly warned that counterfeit pills made to look like real prescription medicines can contain fentanyl or other powerful drugs, sometimes in amounts that can kill. Some pills sold as diazepam in other countries have been found to contain unpredictable "designer" benzodiazepines that are far stronger than expected.

Combining an unknown pill with alcohol stacks two risks on top of each other. If you or someone you know uses pills that didn't come from a pharmacy, keep naloxone on hand and don't use alone. The only Valium you should take is what a pharmacist dispensed to you.

## Other Things That Make the Combination Riskier

Valium plus alcohol is risky on its own. The danger rises further when a third sedating substance joins the mix:

- **Opioid painkillers** such as oxycodone, hydrocodone, codeine, and tramadol. This is the combination behind the FDA boxed warning, and alcohol makes it worse.
- **Sleep medicines,** including zolpidem (Ambien) and over-the-counter "PM" products
- **Sedating antihistamines** such as diphenhydramine (Benadryl) and hydroxyzine. Our page on [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) explains why these are a poor fit after drinking anyway.
- **Other muscle relaxants, gabapentin, or pregabalin.** See our guide to [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).
- **Cannabis,** which adds its own sedation and impairment
- **Medicines that slow how the liver clears diazepam.** Because diazepam is processed by CYP3A4 and CYP2C19, some antifungals, some antibiotics, some heartburn medicines, and certain other drugs can raise its levels. Your pharmacist can check your full list.

Even milder supplements deserve a thought. Melatonin is far less sedating than Valium, but stacking sleep-promoting substances on a night of drinking isn't wise. See our guide to [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol). For a broader look at how supplements and medicines interact, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Dependence and Withdrawal: Don't Stop Suddenly

Two facts surprise many people:

- **Both alcohol and benzodiazepines can cause physical dependence.** If you've taken Valium daily for weeks or longer, your brain adapts to it. The same is true for regular heavy drinking.
- **Stopping either one suddenly can be dangerous.** Withdrawal from benzodiazepines or from heavy daily drinking can cause severe anxiety, shaking, sweating, trouble sleeping, and in some cases seizures.

So if you've been drinking while on Valium and want to change that, **don't stop your Valium abruptly on your own** to make room for drinking, and don't suddenly stop heavy daily drinking without medical advice either. Talk to your prescriber, who can plan a gradual reduction if one is needed. Valium's long half-life means withdrawal symptoms can show up days after the last dose rather than right away, which is another reason to make changes with a doctor.

## Who Should Be Especially Careful

Some people face a higher risk from even small amounts of alcohol with Valium:

- **Adults over 65,** who clear diazepam more slowly and are more prone to falls and confusion. Many geriatric guidelines already advise caution with long-acting benzodiazepines in older adults.
- **People with liver disease,** including liver damage from drinking, because the liver does the work of clearing diazepam
- **People with lung or breathing problems,** such as COPD or sleep apnea, since both substances can slow breathing
- **Anyone also taking opioids** or other sedating medicines
- **People who are pregnant or breastfeeding,** who should talk to their doctor about both Valium and alcohol
- **Anyone who has to drive, operate machinery, or care for children** the next day

## A Note on DHM and Valium

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound sold as a hangover supplement. It's worth being direct about how it relates to Valium, because the overlap is real.

In animal research, DHM appears to act partly at the **GABA-A receptor**, the same system Valium works on. Researchers became interested in it partly because it seemed to blunt some of alcohol's effects in rats. That's an interesting finding, but it hasn't been studied alongside benzodiazepines in people, so there's no good evidence about how DHM and diazepam interact. That's a reason for caution, not reassurance.

Two things are clear:

- **There is no good evidence that DHM, or any supplement, makes it safe to combine Valium and alcohol.** Don't treat it as a safety net.
- **Check with your prescriber or pharmacist before taking DHM** if you take Valium or any other benzodiazepine.

We're deliberately not recommending any supplement on this page, because the only safe plan with Valium is not to combine it with alcohol. If you don't take Valium or other sedating medicines, our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers the research and typical use, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Valium (diazepam) and alcohol both press on the brain's GABA "brake." Together they can cause heavy sedation, blackouts, falls, slowed breathing, and in the worst cases death.
- Valium lasts much longer than many other anxiety pills. Diazepam and its active by-product can stay in your system for days, so waiting overnight isn't enough.
- Don't drink on days you take Valium, be cautious for at least a day or two after a single dose, and ask your prescriber what applies to you.
- Don't use Valium for hangover anxiety, and skip the drinks if you've taken it for a flight.
- Never take pills that didn't come from a pharmacy.
- If someone is hard to wake or breathing slowly after mixing them, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Valium?**

It's best not to. Valium (diazepam) and alcohol both slow the brain through the same GABA system, and together they can cause much stronger sedation, memory loss, and slowed breathing than either alone. The official label tells patients to avoid alcohol. If you think you might drink while on Valium, talk to your prescriber first.

**How long after taking Valium can I drink alcohol?**

There's no single safe number, and it's longer than most people expect. Diazepam has a half-life of up to about two days, and its active by-product lasts longer still, so it stays in your body for days. If you take it daily, you're always on it. After a single dose, many clinicians would advise waiting at least 24 to 48 hours, longer for older adults or people with liver problems. Ask your prescriber what applies to you.

**Is diazepam and alcohol the same risk as Valium and alcohol?**

Yes. Diazepam is the drug and Valium is one brand name for it. Generic diazepam tablets, liquid, rectal gel, and nasal spray all contain the same medicine and carry the same warning to avoid alcohol.

**Can I take Valium after drinking alcohol?**

No. Alcohol may still be in your blood for hours, so you'd be combining them. Wait until the alcohol is fully out of your system, and don't use Valium to calm hangover anxiety. If you feel shaky and anxious after heavy daily drinking, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor.

**Can I have a drink on a plane if I took Valium for a fear of flying?**

It's better not to. The combination is more sedating than either alone, you need to stay alert enough to follow crew instructions and move around, and the diazepam will still be in your system when you land. Ask your prescriber about timing your dose, and stick to water on travel day.

**What happens if you mix Valium and alcohol?**

Effects range from strong drowsiness, poor coordination, slurred speech, and memory gaps to, at higher amounts, very slow or stopped breathing, choking on vomit, coma, and death. How strongly the two combine is hard to predict and depends on dose, timing, age, body size, food, and other sedating substances involved.

**What are the signs of a Valium and alcohol overdose?**

Call 911 if someone can't be woken, is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, has a very slow pulse, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. Stay with them, roll them onto their side if they're breathing but unresponsive, and give naloxone if opioids or a non-pharmacy pill could be involved.

**Is Valium safer with alcohol than Xanax because it's milder?**

No. Valium may feel gentler to some people, but it acts on the same GABA-A receptor as Xanax and carries the same core risk with alcohol. Because it lasts much longer, it can actually overlap with drinking for days after a dose.

**Can I take DHM if I'm on Valium?**

Check with your prescriber or pharmacist first. In animal studies DHM appears to act partly at GABA-A receptors, the same system Valium works on, and its interaction with diazepam in people hasn't been studied. There is also no good evidence that DHM or any supplement makes it safe to combine Valium and alcohol.
